passages.title: Campaigns and remaining peoples
passages.summary: After Joshua dies, Israel asks the LORD who should fight first. Judah goes up with Simeon and defeats Adoni-Bezek. Caleb’s daughter Achsah again receives her springs. Judah takes the hill country but cannot drive out the plain’s iron chariots. Benjamin does not drive the Jebusites from Jerusalem. Joseph’s house takes Bethel with help from a man of the city. Manasseh, Ephraim, Zebulun, Asher, and Naphtali leave Canaanites in their towns. When Israel grows strong, it puts them to forced labor.
passages.uncertainty: The points show the towns and regions the chapter names. Many locations are approximate.

lds.text: Which tribes drive out their neighbors? Which leave them in place or force them to work (verses 27–33)?

contextNote.title: Remaining peoples complicate the conquest account
contextNote.text: The chapter starts with victories and ends with a list of failures. Verses 27–33 repeat one phrase for five tribes: they “didn’t drive out” the people. Verse 28 adds what Israel did when it was strong enough to finish. It chose forced labor over the command. In verse 34 the Amorites even push Dan into the hills. Chapter 2:1–3 gives the LORD’s response to this.

passages.title: The recurring cycle
passages.summary: The LORD’s angel comes to Bochim and says Israel has not obeyed. So the nations will stay as thorns and their gods as a snare. The people weep. The account then looks back: Israel served the LORD while Joshua and the elders lived. A new generation arose that did not know the LORD or his works. They served the Baals, and the LORD gave them to raiders. He raised up judges to save them, but after each judge they turned back. So the LORD left the nations to test Israel.
passages.uncertainty: The points show the towns and regions the chapter names. Many locations are approximate.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies repentance and the Lord’s repeated willingness to receive people who return. What did the new generation not know (verse 10)?

contextNote.title: A generation change becomes a problem of memory
contextNote.text: Verse 7 says Israel served the LORD while people lived who “had seen” his work. Verse 10 says the next generation “didn’t know the LORD” or what he had done. The text does not say they were told and refused. It says they did not know. Deuteronomy 6:7 and Joshua 4:6–7 had ordered parents to tell the story. Verses 11–19 then lay out the cycle the book will repeat. The trouble begins as a failure of memory between parents and children.

passages.title: Othniel, Ehud, and Shamgar
passages.summary: The LORD leaves several nations to test Israel. Israel marries among them and serves their gods. A king of Mesopotamia rules them eight years, and Othniel, of Caleb’s family, saves them. Then Eglon king of Moab rules Israel eighteen years. The LORD raises up Ehud, a left-handed man of Benjamin. Ehud hides a sword on his right thigh and kills Eglon in private. He escapes, calls Israel to fight, and Moab is subdued. Shamgar later kills six hundred Philistines with an ox goad.
passages.uncertainty: The points show the towns and regions the chapter names. Many locations are approximate.

lds.text: The older Church manual studies Israel’s return to God during trouble. What detail about Ehud does verse 15 give?

contextNote.title: Deliverance uses an unexpected advantage
contextNote.text: Verse 15 calls Ehud “a left-handed man” before he does anything. The detail explains the plan. Ehud straps his sword on the right thigh, under his clothes (verse 16). That is not the side where one would look for a weapon. He draws it with his left hand (verse 21). The text treats a trait that set him apart as the means of rescue. Each rescue in this chapter begins the same way: Israel “cried to the LORD.”

passages.title: Deborah, Barak, and Jael
passages.summary: Israel does evil again, and Jabin king of Canaan oppresses them twenty years. His general Sisera has nine hundred iron chariots. Deborah, a prophetess, judges Israel under a palm tree. She tells Barak that the LORD commands him to gather ten thousand men. Barak will go only if she goes with him. She agrees but says a woman will get the honor. The LORD routs Sisera’s army, and Sisera flees on foot to Jael’s tent. Jael gives him milk and kills him with a tent peg as he sleeps.
passages.uncertainty: The points show the towns and regions the chapter names. Many locations are approximate.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies Deborah’s influence and asks how faith can help other people act. What does Deborah tell Barak about the honor of the victory (verse 9)?

contextNote.title: Victory disrupts expected roles
contextNote.text: Deborah holds two roles in verse 4: prophetess and judge. Barak is the general, yet he will not march without her (verse 8). Verse 9 says the cost: the honor will go to “a woman.” A reader might expect that woman to be Deborah. Verses 17–21 give the victory to Jael, a tent dweller and not an Israelite. Sisera had nine hundred iron chariots and dies by a tent peg. The chapter credits God with the result (verse 23).

passages.title: The song of Deborah
passages.summary: Deborah and Barak sing after the victory. They praise leaders and people who offered themselves willingly. The song recalls empty roads and villages before Deborah arose. It praises the tribes that came: Ephraim, Benjamin, Zebulun, Issachar, and Naphtali. It asks why Reuben, Gilead, Dan, and Asher stayed home. The stars and the river Kishon fought against Sisera. Jael is called most blessed of women for killing him. The song ends with Sisera’s mother waiting at her window for him.
passages.uncertainty: The points show the towns and regions the chapter names. Many locations are approximate.

lds.text: The older manual studies willing service and courage. Read the poem’s celebration beside its depiction of harm. Which tribes stayed away, according to verses 16–17?

contextNote.title: A victory song also judges participation
contextNote.text: The song praises God and also keeps a record of who came. Verses 14–15 and 18 name tribes that risked their lives. Verses 16–17 name those that did not: Reuben, Gilead, Dan, and Asher. Each is pictured at its ordinary work, with flocks or ships. The poem asks them why and gives no excuse. Verse 23 curses a town that would not help. The poem closes with an enemy’s mother waiting, and it lets the reader see her.

passages.title: Gideon’s call
passages.summary: Midian raids Israel for seven years and strips the land at harvest. Israel cries out, and a prophet reminds them they did not listen. The LORD’s angel finds Gideon threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it. He calls Gideon a mighty man and sends him to save Israel. Gideon says his family is the poorest and he is the least. At night he tears down his father’s altar to Baal. His father Joash tells the angry town to let Baal defend himself. Gideon gathers an army and twice asks for a sign with a fleece.
passages.uncertainty: The points show the towns and regions the chapter names. Many locations are approximate.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies trust when God’s instructions differ from what a person expects. Whose altar must Gideon pull down first (verse 25)?

contextNote.title: The first conflict occurs inside Gideon's household
contextNote.text: Gideon’s first task is at home, not on a battlefield. The Baal altar belongs to his own father (verse 25). He does it at night because he fears his family and the town (verse 27). The town demands his death. In verse 31 his father, the altar’s owner, defends him. His argument is simple: a real god can fight for himself. So the first person won over is inside Gideon’s household.

passages.title: Gideon’s reduced force
passages.summary: Gideon camps with thirty-two thousand men. The LORD says they are too many, or Israel will boast that it saved itself. The fearful go home, and ten thousand remain. At the water the LORD keeps only the three hundred who lap from their hands. Gideon sneaks to the enemy camp and hears a man tell a dream of defeat. He gives each man a trumpet, a jar, and a torch. At night they blow, break the jars, and shout. The Midianites turn on each other and flee.
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places Judges names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: The Church lesson studies reliance on God. Why does the LORD shrink Gideon’s army (verse 2)?

contextNote.title: Reduced numbers change the explanation of victory
contextNote.text: Armies want more soldiers, and the LORD orders fewer. Verse 2 gives the reason before the cuts begin. With a large force Israel would say its own hand had saved it. So the number drops from thousands to three hundred (verses 3–7). Their gear is trumpets, jars, and torches, not swords in hand (verse 16). Verse 22 says the LORD turned the enemy’s swords on each other. The size of the army is set so the credit cannot be mistaken.

passages.title: Victory, revenge, and the ephod
passages.summary: Ephraim complains at being called late, and Gideon calms them with praise. He chases two Midianite kings across the Jordan with his tired three hundred. Succoth and Penuel refuse him bread. He captures the kings, then punishes Succoth’s elders and kills the men of Penuel. He kills the two kings for the death of his brothers. Israel asks him to rule, and he says the LORD will rule. But he collects gold earrings and makes an ephod that Israel worships. After his death Israel turns to the Baals and forgets his family.
passages.uncertainty: The points show the towns and regions the chapter names. Many locations are approximate.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies trust. The older manual also warns about the ephod and acknowledges the account’s change after victory. What did Gideon’s ephod become (verse 27)?

contextNote.title: A deliverer's achievement can produce another danger
contextNote.text: Gideon began by tearing down an idol’s altar (6:27). In verse 23 he refuses to be king and says the LORD will rule. His very next act is to ask for gold (verse 24). He makes an ephod, a priestly object, and sets it up in his town. Verse 27 says all Israel went after it and it became “a snare.” Aaron also made an idol from gold earrings (Exodus 32:2–4). The deliverer leaves behind a new thing for Israel to worship.

passages.title: Abimelech and Jotham’s warning
passages.summary: Abimelech, Gideon’s son by a woman of Shechem, asks Shechem to make him ruler. They give him silver, and he hires men and kills his seventy brothers. Only the youngest, Jotham, escapes. Jotham shouts a story from Mount Gerizim about trees choosing a king. The olive, fig, and vine refuse, and the bramble accepts. Three years later Shechem turns against Abimelech. He destroys the city and burns its tower with the people inside. At Thebez a woman drops a millstone on his head, and he dies.
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places Judges names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: The manual studies Jotham’s warning. What does the bramble offer the trees in verse 15, and what does it threaten?

contextNote.title: The tree story examines consent to dangerous rule
contextNote.text: In Jotham’s story the useful trees refuse to rule. Each has oil, fruit, or wine to give and will not leave it. Only the bramble says yes. A bramble has no real shade to offer, and it burns easily. Its speech in verse 15 offers “refuge” and threatens fire in the same breath. Jotham applies it to Shechem: they chose a killer as king (verses 16–20). Verses 49 and 57 report that fire did come on Shechem.

passages.title: Tola, Jair, and renewed distress
passages.summary: Tola judges Israel twenty-three years, and Jair twenty-two. Israel again serves the gods of the nations around it. The LORD gives them to the Philistines and Ammonites for eighteen years. Israel cries out and admits its sin. The LORD lists his past rescues and says he will save them no more. He tells them to cry to the gods they chose. Israel confesses again, puts away the foreign gods, and serves the LORD. He can bear their misery no longer, and Ammon gathers for war.
passages.uncertainty: The points show the towns and regions the chapter names. Many locations are approximate.

lds.text: The manual studies the return to God. What did Israel do in verse 16 after the LORD’s answer?

contextNote.title: Confession cannot function as a quick transaction
contextNote.text: Israel’s first confession in verse 10 is quick. The LORD’s answer in verses 11–14 is a refusal. He has rescued them many times, and each time they left. Verse 14 tells them to ask their chosen gods for help. The second confession adds two things (verses 15–16). They accept whatever God decides, and they put the foreign gods away. Only then does the text say his soul was grieved for their misery.

passages.title: Jephthah and his daughter
passages.summary: Jephthah is a strong fighter, but his brothers drive him out as a prostitute’s son. When Ammon attacks, the elders of Gilead ask him to lead them. He agrees on condition that he stay their head. He sends Ammon’s king a long case from history that Israel took no Ammonite land. The king does not listen. Jephthah vows to offer whatever first comes from his house if he wins. He wins, and his only daughter comes out dancing to meet him. She asks two months to mourn, and he does to her as he vowed.
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places Judges names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: The older manual reads the vow as lifelong service. Hayes reads it as sacrifice. The readings differ over the daughter’s fate. What does Jephthah say when he sees her (verse 35)?

contextNote.title: A vow can expose failed judgment
contextNote.text: The LORD’s Spirit is already on Jephthah in verse 29. He still adds a vow in verses 30–31, as if a bargain were needed. The vow is loose: “whatever comes out” of his door. His daughter comes out, as women did to greet victors (Exodus 15:20). In verse 35 he says she has brought him low. The words put the weight on her, though the vow was his. The text never says God asked for this vow or approved it.

passages.title: Conflict at the river
passages.summary: The men of Ephraim are angry that Jephthah fought Ammon without them. They threaten to burn his house. Jephthah says he called and they did not come. Gilead fights Ephraim and takes the Jordan crossings. Each fleeing man is told to say “Shibboleth.” An Ephraimite says “Sibboleth” and is killed. Forty-two thousand of Ephraim die. Jephthah judges six years, and Ibzan, Elon, and Abdon follow him.
passages.uncertainty: The points show the towns and regions the chapter names. Many locations are approximate.

lds.text: The manual compares the conflict with Gideon’s earlier response. How did Gideon answer Ephraim’s complaint in 8:1–3?

contextNote.title: A speech difference becomes a weapon
contextNote.text: Ephraim made the same complaint to Gideon in 8:1. Gideon answered softly, and the anger passed. Jephthah answers with a charge and then with war (verses 2–4). The test at the river in verse 6 uses one word. A small difference in speech marks a man as the enemy. These are Israelites killing Israelites, tribe against tribe. The count in verse 6 is forty-two thousand of their own people.

passages.title: Samson’s birth announced
passages.summary: Israel does evil, and the Philistines rule them forty years. The LORD’s angel appears to the childless wife of Manoah of Dan. She will bear a son who must be a Nazirite from birth. She must drink no wine, and no razor may touch his head. Manoah prays for the man to return, and the angel comes again to the woman. Manoah offers a goat, and the angel goes up in the altar flame. Manoah fears they will die for seeing God. His wife says God would not accept their offering and then kill them.
passages.uncertainty: The points show the towns and regions the chapter names. Many locations are approximate.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies covenant faithfulness. The manual treats the angel as God’s messenger rather than naming him as Christ. How does Manoah’s wife answer his fear in verse 23?

contextNote.title: The mother interprets the encounter more clearly
contextNote.text: The angel comes to the woman both times, not to Manoah (verses 3 and 9). She is never named, yet she receives the message and the rules. Manoah asks for a repeat and then for the angel’s name. In verse 22 he concludes they will die. His wife answers with three plain reasons in verse 23. God took their offering, showed them these things, and told them of a son. She reads the event correctly while her husband panics.

passages.title: The wedding and the riddle
passages.summary: Samson sees a Philistine woman in Timnah and demands her as his wife. His parents object, not knowing the LORD is seeking an occasion against the Philistines. On the way Samson tears a young lion apart with his hands. Later he finds honey in its carcass and eats it. At his wedding feast he bets thirty guests they cannot solve his riddle. They threaten to burn his wife and her father’s house unless she gets the answer. She weeps until Samson tells her, and she tells them. Samson kills thirty men to pay the bet, and his wife is given away.

contextNote.title: A contest exposes someone with less power
contextNote.text: The riddle is a contest between Samson and thirty men. In verse 15 the men turn on the one person outside the bet. They threaten to burn the bride and her father’s house. She has no protector, since her husband is on the other side. She weeps for seven days until he tells her (verse 17). Samson then blames her in verse 18. In 15:6 the Philistines burn her and her father anyway.

passages.title: Retaliation at Lehi
passages.summary: Samson returns for his wife and learns she was given to another man. He ties torches to three hundred foxes and burns the Philistines’ grain. The Philistines burn his wife and her father. Samson strikes them down and hides in a rock cleft. Three thousand men of Judah come to hand him over. He lets them bind him, then snaps the ropes when the Spirit comes on him. He kills a thousand men with a donkey’s jawbone. He is thirsty and calls on the LORD, and God opens a spring.

contextNote.title: Retaliation spreads beyond its original dispute
contextNote.text: Each side in this chapter says it is only paying back. Samson says so in verses 3 and 7, and the Philistines in verse 10. In verse 11 Samson says he did to them as they did to him. The first victims in verse 6 are the woman and her father. They are burned for a wrong done to them, not by them. Judah’s men then side with their rulers against Samson (verse 11). No one in the chapter stops the chain; it only grows.

passages.summary: Samson visits a prostitute in Gaza and carries off the city gates at midnight. He loves Delilah, and Philistine lords pay her to learn his secret. Three times he lies to her, and each time she tests it. She presses him daily until he tells her about his uncut hair. She has his head shaved while he sleeps, and the LORD leaves him. The Philistines blind him and make him grind grain in prison. At a feast for their god Dagon they bring him out for sport. He prays, pushes down the two pillars, and dies with them.

contextNote.title: The final victory comes after loss of control
contextNote.text: Until now Samson has acted by his own strength and for his own reasons. In verse 20 he does not know the LORD has left him. The Philistines take his eyes, which led him from the start (14:1). Verse 28 is only his second recorded prayer (15:18 is the first). He asks to be remembered and strengthened “only this once.” His stated reason is still personal: revenge for his two eyes. Verse 30 says he killed more in his death than in his life.

passages.title: The woman at Gibeah
passages.summary: A Levite’s concubine leaves him and returns to her father in Bethlehem. He goes to bring her back and is kept there for days. On the way home they pass a foreign town and reach Gibeah of Benjamin. Only an old man takes them in. Men of the city surround the house and demand the Levite. He pushes his concubine out to them, and they abuse her all night. In the morning she lies dead at the door. He cuts her body into twelve pieces and sends them through Israel.

contextNote.title: The final violence reaches inside Israel
contextNote.text: The travelers pass Jebus because it is not an Israelite town (verse 12). They expect safety among their own people in Gibeah. What happens there copies Sodom in Genesis 19. This time no angel steps in, and the woman is handed out. The Levite who gave her up is the one who reports the crime. Verse 30 says nothing like it had been seen since Egypt. The woman is never named and never speaks.

passages.summary: All Israel gathers at Mizpah, four hundred thousand armed men. The Levite tells what Gibeah did but leaves out his own part. The tribes demand that Benjamin hand over the guilty men. Benjamin refuses and gathers its army. Israel asks God who should go first and loses twenty-two thousand men. They weep, ask again, and lose eighteen thousand more. After fasting and offerings, they set an ambush and win on the third day. Benjamin loses twenty-five thousand men, and only six hundred escape.

contextNote.title: The assembly acts on a selective report
contextNote.text: The assembly hears one witness, the Levite (verses 4–6). He says the men of Gibeah meant to kill him. He does not say he put the woman outside himself (19:25). On that account he asks all Israel for a verdict (verse 7). The tribes swear to act before anyone questions him. Benjamin’s refusal in verse 13 then turns a trial into a war. By verse 48 Israel is burning Benjamin’s towns and killing all in them.

passages.summary: Israel had sworn not to give daughters to Benjamin. Now the people weep that a tribe is nearly gone. Six hundred Benjamite men survive and need wives. Israel finds that Jabesh Gilead sent no one to the assembly. They kill its people and take four hundred young women for Benjamin. That is not enough. The elders tell the remaining men to seize dancers at the Shiloh feast. The book ends: there was no king, and everyone did what seemed right.

contextNote.title: A proposed repair repeats harm against women
contextNote.text: Israel made two oaths in anger and now feels trapped (verses 1 and 5). The leaders look for ways around their own words. One oath is kept by destroying Jabesh Gilead (verses 10–11). The other is dodged by letting women be taken, not “given” (verse 22). The elders prepare a legal excuse for the fathers in advance. No one asks the women of Jabesh or Shiloh. The last verse judges all of it: everyone did what seemed right.

events.title: Campaigns and remaining peoples
events.summary: After Joshua dies, Israel asks the LORD who should fight first. Judah goes up with Simeon and defeats Adoni-Bezek. Caleb’s daughter Achsah again receives her springs. Judah takes the hill country but cannot drive out the plain’s iron chariots. Benjamin does not drive the Jebusites from Jerusalem. Joseph’s house takes Bethel with help from a man of the city. Manasseh, Ephraim, Zebulun, Asher, and Naphtali leave Canaanites in their towns. When Israel grows strong, it puts them to forced labor.
events.detail: The chapter starts with victories and ends with a list of failures. Verses 27–33 repeat one phrase for five tribes: they “didn’t drive out” the people. Verse 28 adds what Israel did when it was strong enough to finish. It chose forced labor over the command. In verse 34 the Amorites even push Dan into the hills. Chapter 2:1–3 gives the LORD’s response to this.

events.title: The recurring cycle
events.summary: The LORD’s angel comes to Bochim and says Israel has not obeyed. So the nations will stay as thorns and their gods as a snare. The people weep. The account then looks back: Israel served the LORD while Joshua and the elders lived. A new generation arose that did not know the LORD or his works. They served the Baals, and the LORD gave them to raiders. He raised up judges to save them, but after each judge they turned back. So the LORD left the nations to test Israel.

The text does not say they were told and refused. It says they did not know. Deuteronomy 6:7 and Joshua 4:6–7 had ordered parents to tell the story. events.title: Othniel, Ehud, and Shamgar
events.summary: The LORD leaves several nations to test Israel. Israel marries among them and serves their gods. events.title: Deborah, Barak, and Jael

Sisera had nine hundred iron chariots and dies by a tent peg. The chapter credits God with the result (verse 23).

events.title: The song of Deborah
events.summary: Deborah and Barak sing after the victory. They praise leaders and people who offered themselves willingly. The song recalls empty roads and villages before Deborah arose. It praises the tribes that came: Ephraim, Benjamin, Zebulun, Issachar, and Naphtali. It asks why Reuben, Gilead, Dan, and Asher stayed home. The stars and the river Kishon fought against Sisera. Jael is called most blessed of women for killing him. The song ends with Sisera’s mother waiting at her window for him.
events.detail: The song praises God and also keeps a record of who came. Verses 14–15 and 18 name tribes that risked their lives. Verses 16–17 name those that did not: Reuben, Gilead, Dan, and Asher. Each is pictured at its ordinary work, with flocks or ships. The poem asks them why and gives no excuse. Verse 23 curses a town that would not help. The poem closes with an enemy’s mother waiting, and it lets the reader see her.

events.title: Gideon’s call
events.summary: Midian raids Israel for seven years and strips the land at harvest. Israel cries out, and a prophet reminds them they did not listen. The LORD’s angel finds Gideon threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it. He calls Gideon a mighty man and sends him to save Israel. Gideon says his family is the poorest and he is the least. At night he tears down his father’s altar to Baal. His father Joash tells the angry town to let Baal defend himself. Gideon gathers an army and twice asks for a sign with a fleece.
events.detail: Gideon’s first task is at home, not on a battlefield. The Baal altar belongs to his own father (verse 25). He does it at night because he fears his family and the town (verse 27). The town demands his death. In verse 31 his father, the altar’s owner, defends him. His argument is simple: a real god can fight for himself. So the first person won over is inside Gideon’s household.

events.title: Gideon’s reduced force
events.summary: Gideon camps with thirty-two thousand men. The LORD says they are too many, or Israel will boast that it saved itself. The fearful go home, and ten thousand remain. At the water the LORD keeps only the three hundred who lap from their hands. Gideon sneaks to the enemy camp and hears a man tell a dream of defeat. He gives each man a trumpet, a jar, and a torch. At night they blow, break the jars, and shout. The Midianites turn on each other and flee.
events.detail: Armies want more soldiers, and the LORD orders fewer. Verse 2 gives the reason before the cuts begin. With a large force Israel would say its own hand had saved it. So the number drops from thousands to three hundred (verses 3–7). Their gear is trumpets, jars, and torches, not swords in hand (verse 16). Verse 22 says the LORD turned the enemy’s swords on each other. The size of the army is set so the credit cannot be mistaken.

events.title: Victory, revenge, and the ephod
events.summary: Ephraim complains at being called late, and Gideon calms them with praise. He chases two Midianite kings across the Jordan with his tired three hundred. Succoth and Penuel refuse him bread. He captures the kings, then punishes Succoth’s elders and kills the men of Penuel. He kills the two kings for the death of his brothers. Israel asks him to rule, and he says the LORD will rule. But he collects gold earrings and makes an ephod that Israel worships. After his death Israel turns to the Baals and forgets his family.
events.detail: Gideon began by tearing down an idol’s altar (6:27). In verse 23 he refuses to be king and says the LORD will rule. His very next act is to ask for gold (verse 24). He makes an ephod, a priestly object, and sets it up in his town. Verse 27 says all Israel went after it and it became “a snare.” Aaron also made an idol from gold earrings (Exodus 32:2–4). The deliverer leaves behind a new thing for Israel to worship.

events.title: Abimelech and Jotham’s warning
events.summary: Abimelech, Gideon’s son by a woman of Shechem, asks Shechem to make him ruler. They give him silver, and he hires men and kills his seventy brothers. Only the youngest, Jotham, escapes. Jotham shouts a story from Mount Gerizim about trees choosing a king. The olive, fig, and vine refuse, and the bramble accepts. Three years later Shechem turns against Abimelech. He destroys the city and burns its tower with the people inside. At Thebez a woman drops a millstone on his head, and he dies.
events.detail: In Jotham’s story the useful trees refuse to rule. Each has oil, fruit, or wine to give and will not leave it. Only the bramble says yes. A bramble has no real shade to offer, and it burns easily. Its speech in verse 15 offers “refuge” and threatens fire in the same breath. Jotham applies it to Shechem: they chose a killer as king (verses 16–20). Verses 49 and 57 report that fire did come on Shechem.

events.title: Tola, Jair, and renewed distress
events.summary: Tola judges Israel twenty-three years, and Jair twenty-two. Israel again serves the gods of the nations around it. The LORD gives them to the Philistines and Ammonites for eighteen years. Israel cries out and admits its sin. The LORD lists his past rescues and says he will save them no more. He tells them to cry to the gods they chose. Israel confesses again, puts away the foreign gods, and serves the LORD. He can bear their misery no longer, and Ammon gathers for war.

Verse 14 tells them to ask their chosen gods for help. The second confession adds two things (verses 15–16). They accept whatever God decides, and they put the foreign gods away. Only then does the text say his soul was grieved for their misery.

events.title: Jephthah and his daughter
events.summary: Jephthah is a strong fighter, but his brothers drive him out as a prostitute’s son. When Ammon attacks, the elders of Gilead ask him to lead them. He agrees on condition that he stay their head. He sends Ammon’s king a long case from history that Israel took no Ammonite land. The king does not listen. Jephthah vows to offer whatever first comes from his house if he wins. He wins, and his only daughter comes out dancing to meet him. She asks two months to mourn, and he does to her as he vowed.

His daughter comes out, as women did to greet victors (Exodus 15:20). In verse 35 he says she has brought him low. The words put the weight on her, though the vow was his. The text never says God asked for this vow or approved it.

events.title: Conflict at the river
events.summary: The men of Ephraim are angry that Jephthah fought Ammon without them. They threaten to burn his house. Jephthah says he called and they did not come. Gilead fights Ephraim and takes the Jordan crossings. Each fleeing man is told to say “Shibboleth.” An Ephraimite says “Sibboleth” and is killed. Forty-two thousand of Ephraim die. Jephthah judges six years, and Ibzan, Elon, and Abdon follow him.
events.detail: Ephraim made the same complaint to Gideon in 8:1. Gideon answered softly, and the anger passed. Jephthah answers with a charge and then with war (verses 2–4). The test at the river in verse 6 uses one word. A small difference in speech marks a man as the enemy. These are Israelites killing Israelites, tribe against tribe. The count in verse 6 is forty-two thousand of their own people.

events.summary: Israel does evil, and the Philistines rule them forty years. The LORD’s angel appears to the childless wife of Manoah of Dan. She will bear a son who must be a Nazirite from birth. She must drink no wine, and no razor may touch his head. Manoah prays for the man to return, and the angel comes again to the woman. Manoah offers a goat, and the angel goes up in the altar flame. Manoah fears they will die for seeing God. His wife says God would not accept their offering and then kill them.

Manoah asks for a repeat and then for the angel’s name. In verse 22 he concludes they will die. His wife answers with three plain reasons in verse 23. God took their offering, showed them these things, and told them of a son. She reads the event correctly while her husband panics.

Samson kills thirty men to pay the bet, and his wife is given away.

events.title: The woman at Gibeah
events.summary: A Levite’s concubine leaves him and returns to her father in Bethlehem. He goes to bring her back and is kept there for days. On the way home they pass a foreign town and reach Gibeah of Benjamin. Only an old man takes them in. Men of the city surround the house and demand the Levite. He pushes his concubine out to them, and they abuse her all night. In the morning she lies dead at the door. He cuts her body into twelve pieces and sends them through Israel.
events.detail: The travelers pass Jebus because it is not an Israelite town (verse 12). They expect safety among their own people in Gibeah. What happens there copies Sodom in Genesis 19. This time no angel steps in, and the woman is handed out. The Levite who gave her up is the one who reports the crime. Verse 30 says nothing like it had been seen since Egypt. The woman is never named and never speaks.

lds.text: The older Church manual describes the harm caused by Israel’s loss of moral care. What do those who see the Levite’s message say (verse 30)?

events.title: War against Benjamin
events.summary: All Israel gathers at Mizpah, four hundred thousand armed men. The Levite tells what Gibeah did but leaves out his own part. The tribes demand that Benjamin hand over the guilty men. Benjamin refuses and gathers its army. Israel asks God who should go first and loses twenty-two thousand men. They weep, ask again, and lose eighteen thousand more. After fasting and offerings, they set an ambush and win on the third day. Benjamin loses twenty-five thousand men, and only six hundred escape.
events.detail: The assembly hears one witness, the Levite (verses 4–6). He says the men of Gibeah meant to kill him. He does not say he put the woman outside himself (19:25). On that account he asks all Israel for a verdict (verse 7). The tribes swear to act before anyone questions him. Benjamin’s refusal in verse 13 then turns a trial into a war. By verse 48 Israel is burning Benjamin’s towns and killing all in them.

lds.text: The manual describes the near destruction of Benjamin. Compare the Levite’s report in verses 4–6 with 19:25. What does he leave out?

events.title: Women taken and the closing refrain
events.summary: Israel had sworn not to give daughters to Benjamin. Now the people weep that a tribe is nearly gone. Six hundred Benjamite men survive and need wives. Israel finds that Jabesh Gilead sent no one to the assembly. They kill its people and take four hundred young women for Benjamin. That is not enough. The elders tell the remaining men to seize dancers at the Shiloh feast. The book ends: there was no king, and everyone did what seemed right.
events.detail: Israel made two oaths in anger and now feels trapped (verses 1 and 5). The leaders look for ways around their own words. One oath is kept by destroying Jabesh Gilead (verses 10–11). The other is dodged by letting women be taken, not “given” (verse 22). The elders prepare a legal excuse for the fathers in advance. No one asks the women of Jabesh or Shiloh. The last verse judges all of it: everyone did what seemed right.

ancientRoads.title: International coastal highway
ancientRoads.summary: This major route linked Egypt with the coast and northern Levant. Traders, messengers, and imperial armies used its plains and passes.
ancientRoads.detail: The southern section followed the coast through Gaza and Philistia. Farther north, important branches crossed Carmel and the Jezreel Valley. “Via Maris” is a familiar later name. This guide calls it the international coastal highway.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Strong evidence supports this route. The line shows a general path. Its branches and exact roadbeds changed over time.

ancientRoads.title: Jezreel Valley–Damascus route
ancientRoads.summary: This branch connected Megiddo and the Jezreel Valley with Beth Shean. It continued toward the upper Jordan region and Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: The valley and its crossings supported trade and army travel. The route joined the coast, Galilee, Transjordan, and inland Syria.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The main connection is well supported. The line shows a broad route, not one fixed or fully built road.

ancientRoads.title: Central ridge road
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south road followed the central hills. It passed Beersheba, Hebron, Jerusalem, Bethel, and Shechem. It continued toward the Jezreel Valley.
ancientRoads.detail: This route linked the principal highland settlements of Judah and Israel. It avoided some lowland obstacles but still depended on ridges, saddles, and local descents. Judges 21:19 names a highway that goes up from Bethel to Shechem.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The hill route is well supported. The exact track could divide or shift between nearby ridges and towns.

ancientRoads.title: Jordan Valley and Arabah route
ancientRoads.summary: A long north–south route used the Arabah and Jordan Valley. It joined Aqaba, the Dead Sea, Jericho, Beth Shean, and Galilee.
ancientRoads.detail: Travelers used several tracks on both sides of the valley. Fords and seasonal conditions affected where people crossed the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The valley route is well supported. The line combines several possible tracks. It does not mark specific river crossings.

ancientRoads.title: Shephelah road
ancientRoads.summary: This route ran through Judah’s western lowlands. It joined Beersheba, Lachish, Gezer, Aphek, and the valleys below Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.detail: The Shephelah formed a connected lowland zone between the coastal plain and the Judean hills. Fortified towns near the route guarded approaches into the highlands.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional route is well supported. Local branches between valleys and fortified towns are simplified.

ancientRoads.title: Beth-horon ascent
ancientRoads.summary: This important western route connected the coastal plain with Jerusalem. It passed through the Aijalon Valley and climbed Beth-horon.
ancientRoads.detail: The ascent used a favorable pass through difficult hill country. It served traffic between the coast, the Benjamin plateau, and Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The pass and connection are well supported. The line does not claim an exact roadbed at every point.

ancientRoads.title: Lachish–Jerusalem approaches
ancientRoads.summary: Routes through the Shephelah valleys connected Lachish with Jerusalem. They also joined nearby walled towns with the Judean hills.
ancientRoads.detail: Second Kings 18:17 sends an Assyrian army from Lachish up to Jerusalem. The text does not name the road. This line shows one common approach.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is probable. The exact track is unknown, so the line is dashed.

ancientRoads.title: Jerusalem–Jericho road
ancientRoads.summary: This steep east–west route connected Jerusalem with Jericho and the Jordan Valley. It also reached crossings toward Transjordan.
ancientRoads.detail: The road descended rapidly through dry and broken terrain. It gave Jerusalem access to the valley and to routes east of the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The connection is well supported. The displayed bends are approximate and do not identify one preserved Iron Age roadbed.

ancientRoads.title: Transjordan plateau route
ancientRoads.summary: A major north–south route crossed the Transjordan plateau. It passed Edom, Moab, Ammon, and Gilead before reaching Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: This series of plateau roads is often called the King’s Highway. It supported trade east of the Jordan. It linked nearby towns with Arabia, Syria, and western crossings.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: This broad route is well known. It was not one fully built road. Its path and local branches remain uncertain.

ancientRoads.title: Damascus–Hamath–Aleppo route
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south inland route connected Damascus with the Orontes valley, Hamath, and Aleppo.
ancientRoads.detail: Aleppo stood where many major routes met. They linked Anatolia, Syria, Palestine, Egypt, Mesopotamia, and the Mediterranean. This line follows the broad route through the Orontes valley, not the desert.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is well supported. The evidence does not show one fixed Iron Age track. The line is dashed.

guides.title: Judges: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Victory disrupts expected roles
steps.text: Deborah holds two roles in verse 4: prophetess and judge. Barak is the general, yet he will not march without her (verse 8). Verse 9 says the cost: the honor will go to “a woman.” A reader might expect that woman to be Deborah. Verses 17–21 give the victory to Jael, a tent dweller and not an Israelite. Sisera had nine hundred iron chariots and dies by a tent peg. The chapter credits God with the result (verse 23).

steps.title: A vow can expose failed judgment
steps.text: The LORD’s Spirit is already on Jephthah in verse 29. He still adds a vow in verses 30–31, as if a bargain were needed. The vow is loose: “whatever comes out” of his door. His daughter comes out, as women did to greet victors (Exodus 15:20). In verse 35 he says she has brought him low. The words put the weight on her, though the vow was his. The text never says God asked for this vow or approved it.

steps.title: The final violence reaches inside Israel
steps.text: The travelers pass Jebus because it is not an Israelite town (verse 12). They expect safety among their own people in Gibeah. What happens there copies Sodom in Genesis 19. This time no angel steps in, and the woman is handed out. The Levite who gave her up is the one who reports the crime. Verse 30 says nothing like it had been seen since Egypt. The woman is never named and never speaks.

chapterMaps.narrative: After Joshua dies, Israel asks the LORD who should fight first. Judah goes up with Simeon and defeats Adoni-Bezek. Caleb’s daughter Achsah again receives her springs. Judah takes the hill country but cannot drive out the plain’s iron chariots. Benjamin does not drive the Jebusites from Jerusalem. Joseph’s house takes Bethel with help from a man of the city. Manasseh, Ephraim, Zebulun, Asher, and Naphtali leave Canaanites in their towns. When Israel grows strong, it puts them to forced labor.

chapterMaps.narrative: The LORD’s angel comes to Bochim and says Israel has not obeyed. So the nations will stay as thorns and their gods as a snare. The people weep. The account then looks back: Israel served the LORD while Joshua and the elders lived. A new generation arose that did not know the LORD or his works. They served the Baals, and the LORD gave them to raiders. He raised up judges to save them, but after each judge they turned back. So the LORD left the nations to test Israel.

chapterMaps.narrative: The LORD leaves several nations to test Israel. Israel marries among them and serves their gods. A king of Mesopotamia rules them eight years, and Othniel, of Caleb’s family, saves them. Then Eglon king of Moab rules Israel eighteen years. The LORD raises up Ehud, a left-handed man of Benjamin. Ehud hides a sword on his right thigh and kills Eglon in private. He escapes, calls Israel to fight, and Moab is subdued. Shamgar later kills six hundred Philistines with an ox goad.

chapterMaps.narrative: Israel does evil again, and Jabin king of Canaan oppresses them twenty years. His general Sisera has nine hundred iron chariots. Deborah, a prophetess, judges Israel under a palm tree. She tells Barak that the LORD commands him to gather ten thousand men. Barak will go only if she goes with him. She agrees but says a woman will get the honor. The LORD routs Sisera’s army, and Sisera flees on foot to Jael’s tent. Jael gives him milk and kills him with a tent peg as he sleeps.

chapterMaps.narrative: Deborah and Barak sing after the victory. They praise leaders and people who offered themselves willingly. The song recalls empty roads and villages before Deborah arose. It praises the tribes that came: Ephraim, Benjamin, Zebulun, Issachar, and Naphtali. It asks why Reuben, Gilead, Dan, and Asher stayed home. The stars and the river Kishon fought against Sisera. Jael is called most blessed of women for killing him. The song ends with Sisera’s mother waiting at her window for him.

The LORD’s angel finds Gideon threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it. He calls Gideon a mighty man and sends him to save Israel. Gideon says his family is the poorest and he is the least. At night he tears down his father’s altar to Baal. His father Joash tells the angry town to let Baal defend himself. Gideon gathers an army and twice asks for a sign with a fleece.

chapterMaps.narrative: Gideon camps with thirty-two thousand men. The LORD says they are too many, or Israel will boast that it saved itself. The fearful go home, and ten thousand remain. At the water the LORD keeps only the three hundred who lap from their hands. Gideon sneaks to the enemy camp and hears a man tell a dream of defeat. He gives each man a trumpet, a jar, and a torch. At night they blow, break the jars, and shout. The Midianites turn on each other and flee.

Succoth and Penuel refuse him bread. He captures the kings, then punishes Succoth’s elders and kills the men of Penuel. He kills the two kings for the death of his brothers. Israel asks him to rule, and he says the LORD will rule. But he collects gold earrings and makes an ephod that Israel worships. After his death Israel turns to the Baals and forgets his family.

chapterMaps.narrative: Abimelech, Gideon’s son by a woman of Shechem, asks Shechem to make him ruler. They give him silver, and he hires men and kills his seventy brothers. Only the youngest, Jotham, escapes. Jotham shouts a story from Mount Gerizim about trees choosing a king. The olive, fig, and vine refuse, and the bramble accepts. Three years later Shechem turns against Abimelech. He destroys the city and burns its tower with the people inside. At Thebez a woman drops a millstone on his head, and he dies.

The LORD gives them to the Philistines and Ammonites for eighteen years. Israel cries out and admits its sin. The LORD lists his past rescues and says he will save them no more. He tells them to cry to the gods they chose. Israel confesses again, puts away the foreign gods, and serves the LORD. He can bear their misery no longer, and Ammon gathers for war.

He agrees on condition that he stay their head. He sends Ammon’s king a long case from history that Israel took no Ammonite land. The king does not listen. Jephthah vows to offer whatever first comes from his house if he wins. He wins, and his only daughter comes out dancing to meet him. She asks two months to mourn, and he does to her as he vowed.

Jephthah judges six years, and Ibzan, Elon, and Abdon follow him.

She will bear a son who must be a Nazirite from birth. She must drink no wine, and no razor may touch his head. Manoah prays for the man to return, and the angel comes again to the woman. Manoah offers a goat, and the angel goes up in the altar flame. Manoah fears they will die for seeing God. His wife says God would not accept their offering and then kill them.

On the way Samson tears a young lion apart with his hands. Later he finds honey in its carcass and eats it. At his wedding feast he bets thirty guests they cannot solve his riddle. They threaten to burn his wife and her father’s house unless she gets the answer. She weeps until Samson tells her, and she tells them. Samson kills thirty men to pay the bet, and his wife is given away.

The Philistines burn his wife and her father. Samson strikes them down and hides in a rock cleft. Three thousand men of Judah come to hand him over. He lets them bind him, then snaps the ropes when the Spirit comes on him. He kills a thousand men with a donkey’s jawbone. He is thirsty and calls on the LORD, and God opens a spring.

Three times he lies to her, and each time she tests it. She presses him daily until he tells her about his uncut hair. She has his head shaved while he sleeps, and the LORD leaves him. The Philistines blind him and make him grind grain in prison. At a feast for their god Dagon they bring him out for sport. He prays, pushes down the two pillars, and dies with them.

Micah has a shrine, an ephod, and household gods, and makes a son his priest. In those days Israel had no king, and everyone did what seemed right. A young Levite from Bethlehem comes looking for a place. Micah hires him for ten pieces of silver a year, clothes, and food. The Levite becomes his priest. The tribes demand that Benjamin hand over the guilty men. Benjamin refuses and gathers its army. Israel asks God who should go first and loses twenty-two thousand men. They weep, ask again, and lose eighteen thousand more. After fasting and offerings, they set an ambush and win on the third day. Benjamin loses twenty-five thousand men, and only six hundred escape.

Israel finds that Jabesh Gilead sent no one to the assembly. They kill its people and take four hundred young women for Benjamin. That is not enough. The elders tell the remaining men to seize dancers at the Shiloh feast. The book ends: there was no king, and everyone did what seemed right.

The priest goes with the stronger party without protest (verse 20). Verse 27 calls the people of Laish “quiet and unsuspecting” when Dan kills them. Verse 30 traces the new shrine’s priests to a grandson of Moses.
